description: Please help ID, I am from the west coast so not familiar with birds in the Atlantic. My guess is an eider? It was alone, swimming in the ocean nearshore.

Several dozen King Eiders moving along the coast. Most staying several hundred yards offshore. Hundreds of Common Eiders also seen but not photographed. They show a great deal of white in the plumage unlike the Kings. This time of year the eiders are mostly in eclipse plumage so not much to look at.

Barrow!? What am I doing in Barrow, Alaska, you ask. Well…it’s like this. I have a friend in Austin named Isaac who is a crazy bird photographer like I am. A couple of months ago he sent me an email saying he wanted to go to Barrow for a long weekend to try to photograph Ross’s Gull, one of the rarest gulls in North America. Apparently the species migrates from Siberia across parts of the Arctic Ocean in early October and sometimes can be seen in numbers in Barrow. I had seen the species once before, in Canada in 1988:
http://www.inaturalist.org/observations/151409
but I thought, what the heck. Sounds like an adventure. Very few birds will be around in Barrow, but we might see some Ross’s Gulls which is a super fine bird. So, to make a long story short, we left Austin at 7 PM October 8 and 18 hours of airplanes and airports later found ourselves in Barrow, Alaska where it was 24 degrees F., with a 20 mph north wind. Just balmy conditions. We will have two and a half days here before heading home. Yeah, I know…totally insane!

This bird was 300+ meters offshore and even with 1000mm of camera lens the images are very poor. I guess it might be a White-winged Scoter, but I'm not sure at all. The white seems to be oddly shaped for a scoter, but the bird was way out and the wind blowing 30 mph. It seems to have an orangish colored bill. It drifted by in the fast wind and current and we lost sight of it soon. Any ID thoughts appreciated.

I don't see eiders often and virtually never in eclipse plumage, so I am hoping some of you eider specialists can tell me what I have here. We have had a number of Kings and Commons that were well offshore but the males seemed identifiable. This group flew by rather close, but fast, but I got a few shots. Is the reddish brown bird with the white borders to the speculum area a Common and the others Kings, or are all these one species. I am, frankly, unsure and would appreciate some help. Thanks.

description:
Continuing rare visitor found by Russ Namitz during 2016 Coos Bay CBC.  Mixed in with Surf Scoters and Common Mergansers on far (west) side of bay about 1,000 meters from the Fossil Point/Stinky Hollow pullout.  Large dark-brown sea duck with white chest and white flank patch near tail.  Large wedge-shaped orangish bill.  Good scope views, but too far for good photos with this equipment.

See also The Records of the Oregon Bird Records Committee, Record No. KIEI-16-15 (A12) Coos Bay, Coos Co., 1 male 18 December 2016 – 1 March 2017 (KFr, NeN, OS; photos by PaO, OS, RuN, KFr). (Old number: 162-16-15).

Female KIEI to the right of the COEI (for scale). A really good find, discovered by Nathaniel Sharp and seen by many birders thanks to him. Note the slimmer build and the differences in bill and head shape (and the uplift to the scapular feathers on the back).

description:
*** Rare vagrant. Found by Don Roberson with the scoter and grebe flock just beyond the waves off Asilomar SB. Possibly the same two birds recently recorded in Ventura Co. (12/25/2022 to 2/5/2023) and San Francisco (2/10). 

Don: "I stopped at gate #7 to look through the large scoter/grebe flock in which Bill Hubick had seen a Long-tailed Duck earlier today. The first bird he saw in the scope was a female-plumaged King Eider. It then dived, came up with a mussel, tussled with a Horned Grebe, ate the mussel (I think), and dived again. This was a very large all-brown sea-duck without any white in the wing when it dove, and I knew immediately it was a King Eider by the shape of the black bill with its rounded 'bill-process' extending up towards the eye, but without the exaggerated length and shape of female Common Eider. The head was a creamy-brown with a whitish 'whoosh' above the dark eye, and somewhat contrasting with the dark (but warm) brown plumage of the upperparts. I posted the bird locally.

It took some time to refind in the scoter flock, but I did just as Rita arrived, and then Bill Hubick arrived thereafter. While Rita was scoping the eider, a second female-plumaged King Eider appeared in this scope! So did the Long-tailed Duck for a moment. Thereafter, we scoped and tried distant photos as the two eiders swam around together in the scoter/grebe flock, then went off by themselves to dive near the surfers in the big breakers, and then returned to the flock. Many other locals arrived to view and photograph the two eiders.

It seems like these two, behaving like a "pair," could be an adult female and a first-winter bird, potentially an offspring? We were aware that two female-plumaged King Eiders had been in Ventura Co., and then San Francisco Co., within the last few weeks.

Follow-up: two female-plumaged King Eiders, staying together, were present at Lake Hattie Reservoir, Wyoming, from 12-18 Nov 2022 (1st WY rec), then at Ventura Pier, VEN, 25 Dec-5 Feb 2023, then at Crissy Field, SF, on 10 Feb 2023, and now here today. These dates are from eBird and may not be the exact arrival-departure dates. The concept of a female and offspring is just hypothesis, and these might be two females together, but it is curious. All prior MTY records are of single birds. Ten records are cited in 'Monterey Birds, 2d,' the most recent one summered at Moss Landing in 1991."
